lines.text: Half of a mountainous island in Southeast Asia, a Portuguese colony, then an occupied land that would not give up. This is how East Timor won its freedom.
Portuguese traders came for sandalwood in the fifteen hundreds, and for centuries the east of Timor was a Portuguese colony.
In 1769 the Portuguese made Dili, on the north coast, their capital.
Xanana Gusmao would lead the resistance from the mountains, and later become the first president of a free nation.
Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo would become bishop of Dili, and a brave voice for his people.
Jose Ramos-Horta would speak for the resistance abroad, and share the Nobel Peace Prize with Belo in 1996.
In 1975, as Portugal left, East Timor declared itself a nation.
Within days, in December 1975, Indonesia invaded. The occupation would last twenty-four years, and perhaps a quarter of the people died.
In 1991 troops opened fire on mourners at the Santa Cruz cemetery in Dili. It was filmed, and the world saw.
In 1999, at last, the people voted, and nearly four in five chose independence.
Violence followed the vote, and the United Nations stepped in to run the country while it rebuilt.
And in May 2002 East Timor became independent, one of the newest nations of the century.
After centuries of rule by others, East Timor finally belongs to its own people.
